# Introduction

Let’s Encrypt is a free, automated, and open Certificate Authority (CA) that aims to make web security more accessible for both individuals and organizations. It's a service of the [Internet Security Research Group](https://www.abetterinternet.org/) (abetterinternet.org). It's a non-profit organization.

In this post, I'll quickly go through how I installed and configured Let’s Encrypt on a Debian-based Linux system.

# Prerequisites

Before you get started, make sure your server meets these prerequisites:

1. It needs to run a web server, like Apache or Nginx.

2. You must have a domain name and point it to your server's IP.

3. Make sure that your domain's DNS is properly configured.

# Installation

First, update your system:

```bash
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade
```

Then install Certbot, which is the offical Let’s Encrypt client. This process will take a few minutes:

```bash
sudo apt install certbot python3-certbot-nginx
```

After the installation, the clients are installed but the plugins are not enabled by default. You need to restart the web server:

```bash
sudo systemctl restart nginx
```

Then you can run Certbot to get your SSL certificate:

```bash
sudo certbot --nginx -d yourdomain.com -d www.yourdomain.com
```

Here, `-d` is for domains, and you can add more by repeating `-d`.

This command will run through a few prompts before it finishes. If everything went well, you'll have a new directory in /etc/letsencrypt/live/yourdomain.com with your SSL certificate files in it.

# Configuration

Ubuntu will prompt you to choose how you want to configure Let’s Encrypt to manage automatic renewal of your SSL certificates and after choosing it will automatically add a cron job to handle this task. It will set up a web server configuration file like `yourdomain.com.conf` in the `/etc/nginx/sites-available` directory.

After running the command, check the status of Certbot:

```bash
sudo systemctl status certbot.timer
```

The directory `/etc/letsencrypt/live/yourdomain.com/` should contain the fullchain.pem and privkey.pem. The first is the SSL certificate and server chain in PEM format, and the second is your private key in PEM format.

You can manually force the renewal process with:

```bash
sudo certbot renew --dry-run
```

And finally, restart Nginx so your changes can take effect:

```bash
sudo systemctl restart nginx
```

Remember to test your setup by visiting https://yourdomain.com to check if the SSL certificate is being served correctly!

# Conclusion

Following these steps, you should have a SSL certificate for your website running on your Debian-based server! I hope this guide will be helpful in getting your site up and running.

Please note that this is a simple guide. Depending on the complexity of your website setup, you might need to tweak it a bit to work correctly. Be sure to check LetsEncrypt’s official documentation for more advanced usage, or contact them for more comprehensive assistance if you run into problems.
